title: Modern Hebrew מִלּוֹן
story: For about seventeen centuries Hebrew was no one’s mother tongue. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda built new words from its own roots and marked his accepted coinages in his dictionary with a small sign. The tomato word he refused to print is the word Hebrew speakers use today.

lines.said: For about seventeen centuries, Hebrew was no one’s mother tongue.
lines.screen: The 1908 title page in ghost, with only מִלּוֹן in ink. A note gives the year the dictionary began to appear.

lines.said: Jews read and wrote it, but many modern things had only phrases for names.
lines.screen: Card 1: בתי עיניים, with the gloss “Eyeglasses were houses for the eyes.”

lines.said: Even a dictionary was called sefer milim, a copy of German Wörterbuch.
lines.screen: ספר מלים prints below. Wörter and buch rise under its two words, joined by hairlines.

lines.said: In 1880 Eliezer Ben-Yehuda wrote that such copies had made Hebrew almost German.
lines.screen: A rule strikes ספר מלים on “such copies.” A note names the weekly and the date.

lines.said: Instead he made milon from mila, which means word.
lines.screen: Card 2: מִלָּה plus the ending ־וֹן makes מִלּוֹן.

lines.said: The letter mem can mark a tool, so he put it before the root for sling and made makle’a, a cannon.
lines.screen: The composing card. מַפְתֵּחַ (key) is the model, the root letters ק ל ע drop into the pattern’s slots, and מַקְלֵעַ stands.

lines.said: In his own dictionary, this sign marks words he coined that people had already accepted.
lines.screen: The title page returns, then the key of signs. The coinage sign lifts off the page in rose.

lines.said: It stands before the bicycle, a word for two wheels modeled on the word for ears.
lines.screen: On p. 110 the sign lands before אָפְנַיִם. The card builds it from אוֹפָן (wheel) with the pair ending of אָזְנַיִם (ears).

lines.said: No one is sure what the prophet Ezekiel meant by khashmal.
lines.screen: The clause from Ezekiel 1:4 is set in Hebrew with its English. הַחַשְׁמַל is underlined.

lines.said: An ancient Greek translation gave it as elektron, so a poet used it for electricity.
lines.screen: ἤλεκτρον prints above the Hebrew. Cut to vol. 4, p. 1806, with “Elektrizität; électricité” isolated.

lines.said: Ben-Yehuda did not mark that word as his own.
lines.screen: The rose sign comes down toward the entry, finds a different printed sign there, and withdraws.

lines.said: Yehiel Michel Pines apparently named the tomato agvaniya, from a root that means desire.
lines.screen: עַגְבָנִיָּה with its root letters ע ג ב in ink and the rest in a lighter tone.

lines.said: Ben-Yehuda found the word immodest and kept it out of his dictionary.
lines.screen: His own word, בַּדּוּרָה, prints below. Crop marks close on the empty place where the sign would stand.

lines.said: Today Hebrew speakers call the tomato by the word he kept out.
lines.screen: בַּדּוּרָה sinks to ghost and עַגְבָנִיָּה stays in ink.
The key of signs. The rose sign comes down and lands on its own row, and the film ends.
